subtype: Approach: linking the chore to something he does anyway [Thinking]
passage: I'm Pallavi, and my little brother Chinmay used to dump his shoes and bag wherever he stood. Amma nagged, and it never worked. Then one day I saw him standing in the hallway, talking to himself. "When I come in and change my clothes, that's the moment. Shoes on the rack, bag on the hook. Same time, same place. Then I won't need to remember." He did it the next day, and the next. Now, when he comes in and pulls off his school shirt, I see him walk straight to the rack. Amma has stopped nagging, and honestly, I have too.

qa.q: Where does Chinmay put his bag?
qa.a: Chinmay puts his bag on the hook.

qa.q: How does Chinmay feel about tying the job to changing his clothes?
qa.a: Chinmay feels confident it will work, because changing clothes happens anyway, so he says he won't need to remember the shoes and bag separately.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Chinmay try, and why?
qa.a: Chinmay could put a picture note above the rack or ask a parent to remind him at first. Either could help until the habit is strong.

qa.q: How does Pallavi see the change in Chinmay?
qa.a: Pallavi watches the routine take hold and notes that Amma has stopped nagging, and admits to stopping too, so Pallavi seems relieved and a little impressed.

grounding: A boy links putting shoes on the rack and the bag on the hook to changing clothes after school, so he forgets less, as seen by a sibling.
